An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. ### 3. Run it natively ```sh bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) bun scripts/build-linux.mjs caltrain # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere ``` A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that is already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set `EXACT_SIM` to its name or UDID (or pass `--sim` to `build.mjs`), and keep the same setting for `agent.mjs ios`. On Linux KMS, `EXACT_ROTATE=0|90|180|270` turns the completed image clockwise. Without it, the connector's `panel orientation` property chooses the angle; an absent property means 0. At 90 or 270 degrees layout uses the swapped mode size. The GPU rotates the image before display. Absolute evdev and VNC coordinates use the inverse transform; relative mouse movement and scrolling keep the user's axes. Agent screenshots show the rotated framebuffer, at the panel mode's size. Their replies give that image's point dimensions and clockwise `rotation` in degrees; comparison maps layout boxes onto those axes. Agent layout and target coordinates remain logical. In a headless Linux host, `EXACT_SIZE` supplies the unrotated panel size in points. Ink blits its retained target before readback; other painters upload their completed pixels for the GPU blit. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. ``` On 2026-10-04, a fresh agent given an earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone, with Hermes installed and Cargo's cache warm, finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds; later builds take a minute or two. ## Three principles 1. **Write the web, ship the platform.** What you write is CSS: its names, its layout model and the browser's fast development loop. What you leave out is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as in an app built by hand for that platform. What you write wins (LLP 1115; [details](#what-is-csss-and-what-is-the-platforms)). 2. **An agent can do the whole loop.** It can create an app, run it on any host, see it, operate it, control its clock and run its tests, with no person watching ([details](#for-agents)). 3. **Fast to start and fast to change.** The budgets below come from `rules/RULES.md`. The gate's is checked on every change and the others every hour. A regression is top priority and is attributed to the commit that caused it ([details](#how-it-stays-fast)). | Budget | Target | |---|---| | Cold start to interactive first frame | 100 ms p50 | | Dev restart, edit to present | 100 ms p50 | | App JavaScript executed before first pixel | none | | Touch one line, rebuild that crate | 30 s | | The blocking gate, warm, after a one-crate edit | 30 s | ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R ``` - **Contract** (`contract/`) is compiled in four passes (syntax, types, analysis, and lowering) into a *plan*: tables and bytecode for the views, state and actions. The web build compiles the plan into its ES module; on native hosts a Rust runner executes it. At build time the plan is *baked*: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - **The runner** (`runner/`) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam: the one boundary where data enters the plan. - **The kernel** (`kernel/`) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched [Taffy](vendor/taffy/EXACT-PATCHES.md). The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - **Hosts** (`host/`) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - **Data sources** sit below the data seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). A source that is one HTTP request can be declared in Contract instead; an app whose sources are all declared links no JavaScript engine on native hosts. Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - **Optional pieces** are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a [game engine](game/README.md) add-on. ### What is CSS's, and what is the platform's The order of precedence is the author, then the platform, then CSS's default. One test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice the difference? If so, the platform's answer wins. - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is `display: block`, `box-sizing: content-box`, `flex-direction: row`, `flex-shrink: 1`, the same as a bare `
`. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: `font-size`, `object-fit`, `text-overflow`, `line-clamp`, `light-dark()`, `env(safe-area-inset-top)`. The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Presentation you leave unsaid is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a `button` is the system's button, and a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the reference for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work in the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are checked behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason, in LLP 1001. For example, Taffy has no `position: static`. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG `foreignObject` on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. ### How it stays fast - **The boot path executes and compiles nothing.** TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - **You pay only for what you use.** GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - **The web gets its own small runtime.** On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB (LLP 1071). - **Edits land in about a tenth of a second.** On a fresh app made by `exact new`, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. ## Contract Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. Its views and actions don't fetch, read files, or run arbitrary code; data sources do that. Here is a complete todo app: a Contract file, a TypeScript file, and a test. This exact app was built for web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator, and its test passed on all three. To try it in an app created with `exact new`, replace `app.contract`, `app.ts` and `app.test.contract` with the examples below. ```contract // app.contract: the view, its state, and what each action changes. It names no colour, // font or control size: each host draws its own heading, field, button, checkbox and list. shape Todo id: string title: string done: bool shape Change count: number component Todos state draft = "" mutation changed as shape Change refreshes todos resource todos = todos() as shape Todo[] derive left = todos.filter(t => not t.done).length action edit(value: string) draft = value action add if draft.trim() != "" send changed = addTodo(draft.trim()) draft = "" action toggle(id: string, done: bool) send changed = setDone(id, done) action remove(id: string) send changed = removeTodo(id) view list appearance="auto" height="100%" section header text `${left} left` role="heading" testId="count" row input value=draft input=edit submit=add placeholder="What needs doing?" aria-label="New todo" testId="new-todo" flex=1 min-width=0 button press=add buttonStyle="filled" testId="add" text "Add" section for t in todos key=t.id row delete=remove(t.id) testId=`todo-${t.id}` input type="checkbox" checked=t.done change=toggle(t.id) aria-label=t.title testId=`toggle-${t.id}` text t.title flex=1 button press=remove(t.id) destructive=true testId=`remove-${t.id}` text "Delete" ``` ```ts // app.ts: keeps the list, and answers what app.contract asks for import type { Answer, Sources } from './app.contract.d.ts'; export const grants = ''; // e.g. 'net.fetch https://api.example.com' type Todo = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }; let todos: Todo[] = []; let next = 1; const sources: Sources = { todos: () => todos, addTodo: ([title]) => { todos = [...todos, { id: String(next++), title, done: false }]; return { count: todos.length }; }, setDone: ([id, done]) => { todos = todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native); ``` ```contract-test // app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" ```
WebmacOSiOS Simulator
The view never edits the list itself. An action `send`s a *mutation* to a source, `app.ts` changes its data and answers, and `refreshes todos` asks for the list again. Data lives in one place, and every change to it is a named, typed call an agent can see. This list lives in memory. To keep it across launches, give `app.ts` a grant like `sqlite.open app:/data/todos.db` and use `storage.sqlite`, as [Fieldnotes](apps/fieldnotes) does. A source that is one HTTP request needs no `app.ts`: declare it in `app.contract` with its URL, and Contract reads the JSON reply into the shape. The URL's origin is its grant. [The declared-source recipe](docs/recipes/declared-source.md) has whole examples, and [Weather Now](apps/weather-now) is an app built that way. For more, read the complete [guide for humans](docs/contract-for-humans.md), or look things up in the [guide for agents](docs/contract-for-agents.md), the [grammar and vocabulary reference](docs/contract-grammar.md) and the [recipes](docs/recipes/). ### The pieces | Concept | What it is | |---|---| | `shape` | A closed record type. Fields are `number`, `string`, `bool`, another shape, `option`, or `T[]`. | | `component` | A unit of UI. The first one in a file is the root. Components take `props`, can `inject` what an ancestor `provide`s, and can fill a `slot` with `children`. | | `state` | A value the component owns, its type inferred or declared (`state picked: option = none`). Under a `for`, child state belongs to that keyed row. | | `derive` | A value computed from others, recomputed when they change. | | `resource` | Data from a source: `resource x = source(args) as shape T`. When the arguments change, the source is asked again. | | `mutation` / `send` | A change made through a source: `send x = source(args)`. `refreshes r` asks resource `r` again afterward, `pending(x)` and `failed(x)` show progress, and `failure(x)` says why a resource failed. | | `source` | A source declared in `app.contract`: one HTTP request (`url`, `method`, `header`, `body json` or `graphql`, `pointer`) whose JSON reply is read into a shape. | # Agent instructions **Building an app with Exact rather than working on it?** This checkout is the version to use: Exact has no releases, tags or npm package, and an app uses the checkout by path. Make it with `bun scripts/exact.mjs new `. A website (pages served to a browser) reads only `docs/start-here-site.md`; any other app reads `docs/start-here.md`. That guide is the only required reading (LLP 1115 D7). The rest (`docs/contract-for-agents.md`, `docs/agent-pitfalls.md`, `docs/contract-grammar.md`, `docs/reference.md`) is lookup only, by the section its table names: do not read the long guides front to back. `docs/recipes/` answers the common questions in one short file each, `contract vocab ` answers for any tag or property, every `bun exact.mjs --help` names its flags, and `apps/shelf` is a whole app to grep. **Feedback (required when building an app).** When a doc was wrong or missing, a workaround was needed, something took several tries or a command confused you, record it from the app's directory: `bun exact.mjs feedback note ""`. It attaches exact2's commit and the last command's exit code, never output or code. It goes to Expo only as `bun exact.mjs feedback status` says (skip it under `never`); `EXACT_FEEDBACK=0` stops it on the machine (docs/diary.md). Working on exact2 itself: read `rules/RULES.md` and `rules/DEFERRED.md` first; they bind and this file does not. The design record, the LLP corpus, is private: clone `expo/exact-llp` into `llp/`, which this repository ignores (a worktree links its checkout's: `ln -s /llp llp`); there `llp/1000-exact2-root.explainer.md` is the map. Code and docs cite LLPs by number (`LLP 1115 D7`), and a reader without the corpus learns only that the decision is recorded. Push an LLP before the code that cites it. `docs/agent-pitfalls.md` lists verified footguns in writing apps here; add to it when you hit one. Design documents under `llp/research/` are the predecessor's — research, never authority. ## Write the web, ship the platform LLP 1115 (Charlie, 2026-10-09; James's "no tells"). **What the author writes is CSS**: the vocabulary, the layout model, the dev loop. **What the author leaves unsaid is the platform's**: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, presentation, haptics, keyboard and accessibility come out as a hand-built UIKit/SwiftUI app following Apple's guidelines would have them (AppKit on the Mac, and each platform likewise). **What the author writes wins.** Precedence: author > platform > CSS default. One test settles a dispute: *would someone who knows the platform notice?* If so it is a tell, and the platform's answer wins; judge against a hand-built screen on the same OS version, not against Chrome. So layout stays CSS (users cannot perceive it): a bare node is `display: block`, `box-sizing: content-box`, `flex-direction: row`, `flex-shrink: 1`, and the web is the layout parity oracle — a kernel that disagrees with a bare `
` reintroduces the four-disagreeing-default-layers bug class the predecessor had (an unavoidable deviation is declared in `llp/1001-kernel-v1.spec.md`). Names stay CSS (they are what the author writes): `object-fit`, `text-overflow`, `line-clamp`, not `resizeMode`, `ellipsizeMode`, `numberOfLines`; where a common reset (normalize.css, Tailwind's preflight) differs from the raw default, its behaviour is a familiar path too (LLP 1104 D4). Unsaid presentation is the platform's: a `color` a bar button only inherits from the page leaves UIKit's tint. Agents writing apps should therefore say less — structure (a header's heading and buttons, a `tablist`, an `alertdialog`) and leave colours, fonts and metrics to the platform. ## Apple platforms: public API only Exact's Apple hosts use only Apple's public API: the classes, methods, properties, keys and notifications that Apple's SDK headers declare and its documentation describes. App Store review rejects an app that uses anything else ([App Review Guideline 2.5.1](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#software-requirements)). So shipped code calls no private method, reads no undocumented key, and names no private class: it looks none up by name, compares no class's name and holds no literal of one. Find a platform view through public API, such as its accessibility elements, a delegate or a notification. Where public API cannot reach it, do without, and name the known difference in the LLP that owns the feature and in the code. Private API is for development builds only, inside an `#if` on `EXACT_INSPECT` or `EXACT_AGENT`; LLP 1035.003 names the only exceptions. `host/apple/inspect-gate.test.mjs` checks the sources for private class names. ## Numeric typography On graphical hosts, use tabular digits for numeric columns and values that change in place. Use default spacing for prose, ordinary labels and static standalone statistics. Apply it to numeric text, keeping the platform font. See the [guidance and limits](docs/contract-for-agents.md#tabular-numbers). ## Writing For all prose, always: comments, commit messages, guides, LLPs, issues and PR text. This section binds (`rules/RULES.md`, "Agents"). - Write with clarity of mind. A reader should understand it on first reading and find nothing ambiguous. - Say what the reader needs to know about the topic and nothing more. Do not recount history or keep a diary; an alternative not chosen earns a line when it explains the choice.

For Hermes it runs the installer's offline check, which authenticates the receipts, archives, compiler and host/target bytecode pairing. ### 2. Run Caltrain in the browser ```sh git clone https://github.com/expo/exact.git cd exact bun scripts/exact.mjs setup bun host/web/dev.mjs # Caltrain, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ ``` The first run compiles the toolchain, which takes a few minutes. After that, open [`apps/caltrain/app.contract`](apps/caltrain/app.contract), change some text, and save. The page rebuilds and reloads in about a tenth of a second. Add `--lan` to open the same page from a phone on your network. The server answers only to the host names it prints, as a guard against DNS rebinding; a request with any other `Host` gets 421. To share the page through a tunnel such as `tuft host`, name the tunnel's host with `--allow-host ` (repeatable; `name:port` pins a port). An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. ### 3. Run it natively ```sh bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) bun scripts/build-linux.mjs caltrain # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere ``` A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that is already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set `EXACT_SIM` to its name or UDID (or pass `--sim` to `build.mjs`), and keep the same setting for `agent.mjs ios`. On Linux KMS, `EXACT_ROTATE=0|90|180|270` turns the completed image clockwise. Without it, the connector's `panel orientation` property chooses the angle; an absent property means 0. At 90 or 270 degrees layout uses the swapped mode size. The GPU rotates the image before display. Absolute evdev and VNC coordinates use the inverse transform; relative mouse movement and scrolling keep the user's axes. Agent screenshots show the rotated framebuffer, at the panel mode's size. Their replies give that image's point dimensions and clockwise `rotation` in degrees; comparison maps layout boxes onto those axes. Agent layout and target coordinates remain logical. In a headless Linux host, `EXACT_SIZE` supplies the unrotated panel size in points. Ink blits its retained target before readback; other painters upload their completed pixels for the GPU blit. KMS still reads back into dumb buffers. On Linux, a development build can serve its screen over VNC: set `EXACT_VNC=1` and `EXACT_VNC_PASSWORD` to 1–8 bytes. It listens on `127.0.0.1:5900`; `EXACT_VNC=host:port` selects another address. Production bakes ignore both variables. ### 4. Make your own app ```sh bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # the first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator ``` `exact new` creates a standalone app: `app.contract` (the view), `app.ts` (its data), `app.json` (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy) and `app.test.contract` (its test). Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. ``` On 2026-10-04, a fresh agent given an earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone, with Hermes installed and Cargo's cache warm, finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds; later builds take a minute or two. ## Three principles 1. **Write the web, ship the platform.** What you write is CSS: its names, its layout model and the browser's fast development loop. What you leave out is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as in an app built by hand for that platform. What you write wins (LLP 1115; [details](#what-is-csss-and-what-is-the-platforms)). 2. **An agent can do the whole loop.** It can create an app, run it on any host, see it, operate it, control its clock and run its tests, with no person watching ([details](#for-agents)). 3. **Fast to start and fast to change.** The budgets below come from `rules/RULES.md`. The gate's is checked on every change and the others every hour. A regression is top priority and is attributed to the commit that caused it ([details](#how-it-stays-fast)). | Budget | Target | |---|---| | Cold start to interactive first frame | 100 ms p50 | | Dev restart, edit to present | 100 ms p50 | | App JavaScript executed before first pixel | none | | Touch one line, rebuild that crate | 30 s | | The blocking gate, warm, after a one-crate edit | 30 s | ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R ``` - **Contract** (`contract/`) is compiled in four passes (syntax, types, analysis, and lowering) into a *plan*: tables and bytecode for the views, state and actions. The web build compiles the plan into its ES module; on native hosts a Rust runner executes it. At build time the plan is *baked*: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - **The runner** (`runner/`) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam: the one boundary where data enters the plan. - **The kernel** (`kernel/`) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched [Taffy](vendor/taffy/EXACT-PATCHES.md). The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - **Hosts** (`host/`) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - **Data sources** sit below the data seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). A source that is one HTTP request can be declared in Contract instead; an app whose sources are all declared links no JavaScript engine on native hosts. Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - **Optional pieces** are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a [game engine](game/README.md) add-on. ### What is CSS's, and what is the platform's The order of precedence is the author, then the platform, then CSS's default. One test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice the difference? If so, the platform's answer wins. - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is `display: block`, `box-sizing: content-box`, `flex-direction: row`, `flex-shrink: 1`, the same as a bare `
`. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: `font-size`, `object-fit`, `text-overflow`, `line-clamp`, `light-dark()`, `env(safe-area-inset-top)`. The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Presentation you leave unsaid is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a `button` is the system's button, and a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the reference for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work in the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are checked behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason, in LLP 1001. For example, Taffy has no `position: static`. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG `foreignObject` on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. ### How it stays fast - **The boot path executes and compiles nothing.** TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - **You pay only for what you use.** GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - **The web gets its own small runtime.** On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB (LLP 1071). - **Edits land in about a tenth of a second.** On a fresh app made by `exact new`, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. ## Contract Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. The view never edits the list itself. An action `send`s a *mutation* to a source, `app.ts` changes its data and answers, and `refreshes todos` asks for the list again. Push an LLP before the code that cites it. `docs/agent-pitfalls.md` lists verified footguns in writing apps here; add to it when you hit one. Design documents under `llp/research/` are the predecessor's — research, never authority. ## Write the web, ship the platform LLP 1115 (Charlie, 2026-10-09; James's "no tells"). **What the author writes is CSS**: the vocabulary, the layout model, the dev loop. **What the author leaves unsaid is the platform's**: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, presentation, haptics, keyboard and accessibility come out as a hand-built UIKit/SwiftUI app following Apple's guidelines would have them (AppKit on the Mac, and each platform likewise). **What the author writes wins.** Precedence: author > platform > CSS default. One test settles a dispute: *would someone who knows the platform notice?* If so it is a tell, and the platform's answer wins; judge against a hand-built screen on the same OS version, not against Chrome. So layout stays CSS (users cannot perceive it): a bare node is `display: block`, `box-sizing: content-box`, `flex-direction: row`, `flex-shrink: 1`, and the web is the layout parity oracle — a kernel that disagrees with a bare `
` reintroduces the four-disagreeing-default-layers bug class the predecessor had (an unavoidable deviation is declared in `llp/1001-kernel-v1.spec.md`). Names stay CSS (they are what the author writes): `object-fit`, `text-overflow`, `line-clamp`, not `resizeMode`, `ellipsizeMode`, `numberOfLines`; where a common reset (normalize.css, Tailwind's preflight) differs from the raw default, its behaviour is a familiar path too (LLP 1104 D4). Unsaid presentation is the platform's: a `color` a bar button only inherits from the page leaves UIKit's tint. Agents writing apps should therefore say less — structure (a header's heading and buttons, a `tablist`, an `alertdialog`) and leave colours, fonts and metrics to the platform. ## Apple platforms: public API only Exact's Apple hosts use only Apple's public API: the classes, methods, properties, keys and notifications that Apple's SDK headers declare and its documentation describes. App Store review rejects an app that uses anything else ([App Review Guideline 2.5.1](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#software-requirements)). So shipped code calls no private method, reads no undocumented key, and names no private class: it looks none up by name, compares no class's name and holds no literal of one. Find a platform view through public API, such as its accessibility elements, a delegate or a notification. Where public API cannot reach it, do without, and name the known difference in the LLP that owns the feature and in the code. Private API is for development builds only, inside an `#if` on `EXACT_INSPECT` or `EXACT_AGENT`; LLP 1035.003 names the only exceptions. `host/apple/inspect-gate.test.mjs` checks the sources for private class names. ## Numeric typography On graphical hosts, use tabular digits for numeric columns and values that change in place. Use default spacing for prose, ordinary labels and static standalone statistics. Apply it to numeric text, keeping the platform font. See the [guidance and limits](docs/contract-for-agents.md#tabular-numbers). ## Writing For all prose, always: comments, commit messages, guides, LLPs, issues and PR text. This section binds (`rules/RULES.md`, "Agents"). - Write with clarity of mind. A reader should understand it on first reading and find nothing ambiguous. - Say what the reader needs to know about the topic and nothing more. Do not recount history or keep a diary; an alternative not chosen earns a line when it explains the choice.

bun exact.mjs linux [--json]
  build the Linux host (test and agent linux drive it headless)

  --json  one JSON object on stdout, its last line: the artifact's path, target, trust (a failure: code, error); the build's own output on stderr

A development build (cargo profile host-dev); prints the binary's path. It runs headless
anywhere, macOS included, with no display.
Ports    none. Runs to completion.
Example  bun exact.mjs linux && bun exact.mjs test linux
bun exact.mjs test [web|ios|macos|linux|windows|android] [<file.test.contract>|<glob>]… [flags]
  run *.test.contract (or the files named) on a host app.json ships

  --size <w>x<h>          viewport; Linux: unrotated panel; 90/270 swap layout
  --sim <udid|name> · --variant <name>  iOS: which simulator (default: booted) · which app variant

Compiles first, a compile error said as contract build says it, so no contract build before
it: web builds the app (web-build); ios, macos and windows build when the build is missing or
older than its sources, saying so on stderr; windows drives at app.json's window size. Each test launches the app fresh with its own
store, after its first data has landed; its leading lines (size, epoch, fail fetch …) override flags. Exit 1 when a test fails.
Host     unnamed: one app.json ships, chosen as verify's (verify --help) and macos or linux too; none here: refused, saying why.
Server   restarts empty per test (DB=.exact/test/db.sqlite; database:false too); an ancestor's stays shared; else refuses a live server or ignored DB.
Runs     to completion; nothing is left running; a test past 30 s says its line every 30 s.
Backend  start snapback4 dev on app.ts’s selected origin’s port first; checked before launch.
         A server this run did not start stays shared. EXACT_PORT is the page’s.
Lines    tap, type, expect text|tree|state|disabled|refusal, clock data|settle|+<ms>|until state …, reload, back, fail|pass
         fetch, answer fetch "<prefix>" with <status> [json], request: docs/recipes/tests.md;
         all: docs/contract-grammar.md "Authored tests".
Example  bun exact.mjs test ios tests/*.test.contract --size 390x844
More     bun exact.mjs test --help all: every flag (--test, --storage, --port, --backend …), the ports
